prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

NEW YORK (CNN) -- Five new cases of the H1N1 virus in New York City schools will force three schools to close for a week, Mayor Michael Bloomberg said at a news conference Thursday evening. The city is temporarily closing the schools to "slow transmission" of the virus, Mayor Michael Bloomberg said. The two intermediate schools and one primary school are in Queens, and all three will be closed for at least five days, the mayor said. "We are closing the schools to slow transmission" of sickness, he said. Bloomberg, flanked by New York Gov. David Paterson and New York City School Chancellor Joel Klein, said four students at one of the intermediate schools have the virus and an administrator was critically ill Thursday with H1N1. Bloomberg indicated the school administrator had a pre-existing medical condition. Fifty students at that school have been sent home with flu-like symptoms since May 6. At the two other schools, the primary school had an overflowing nurse's office Thursday, reporting 29 students suffering from flu-like symptoms. The other intermediate school had 241 students absent with illness Thursday. The New York City Department of Health and the Department of Education have been in nearly constant contact, said Jason Post, a spokesman from Bloomberg's office. When there's a spike in students absent from classes, the Department of Health is alerted. "There's always good communication, flu or no flu," Post said. "But our senses have been sharp for a while now." The Health Department has seen a general increase in flu activity in Queens, officials said in a news release. While the symptoms of H1N1 flu seem to resemble those of seasonal flu, the H1N1 virus appears to spread more extensively, at least in schools, warranting closures to slow transmission in the community, the release said. Dr. Isaac Weisfuse, the deputy commissioner of the city's Department of Hygiene and Mental Health, said although concern is legitimate, there's no solid evidence that suggests the H1N1 flu -- also known as swine flu -- is more dangerous than the flu in general. "The bottom line is if you're sick, stay home," Weisfuse said. "And don't go back to school until you're better for one whole day." In late April, St. Francis Prep, a high school in Queens, was closed because of a flu outbreak. Since then, the school reopened and the stricken students have recovered, according to the mayor's office. "As we have said from the outset of the appearance of H1N1 in our city last month, we will share with New Yorkers what we know and not speculate on what we don't know," said Bloomberg in a statement. According to the World Health Organization and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, as of Thursday night 7,412 cases of H1N1 flu have been confirmed worldwide. The organizations said 63 deaths attributed to the virus have been confirmed worldwide. The CDC said 4,298 cases of the virus and three fatalities have been confirmed in the United States as of Thursday night. New York had 224 confirmed cases of H1N1, the CDC said. It was not clear whether the five cases cited by Bloomberg and the other New York officials were included in the latest CDC total.

NEW YORK (CNN) — New York City will shut down three public schools for at least five days after five additional H1N1 infections were identified, Mayor Michael Bloomberg announced at a Thursday evening news conference.

The temporary closures—affecting two intermediate schools and one primary school in Queens—are intended to reduce the spread of the virus, Bloomberg said.

Appearing alongside New York Gov. David Paterson and city Schools Chancellor Joel Klein, the mayor reported that four students at one intermediate school had contracted H1N1. An administrator at the same school was critically ill with the virus Thursday and had an existing medical condition, Bloomberg indicated. Since May 6, 50 students from that school have been sent home after developing flu-like symptoms.

The primary school’s nurse’s office was overwhelmed Thursday, with 29 students reporting symptoms resembling the flu. At the second intermediate school, 241 students were absent because of illness that day.

Jason Post, a spokesperson for Bloomberg’s office, said the city’s health and education departments had maintained almost continuous communication. The Health Department is notified whenever schools experience an unusual rise in student absences.

“There's always good communication, flu or no flu,” Post said, adding, “But our senses have been sharp for a while now.”

City health officials said in a news release that flu activity had generally increased across Queens. Although H1N1 symptoms appeared similar to those caused by seasonal influenza, the new virus seemed to be spreading more widely—particularly in schools—making closures appropriate as a way to limit community transmission, the release stated.

Dr. Isaac Weisfuse, deputy commissioner of the city’s Department of Hygiene and Mental Health, said public concern was understandable but emphasized that there was no firm evidence showing H1N1, also called swine flu, was more hazardous than influenza overall.

“The bottom line is if you're sick, stay home,” Weisfuse said. He advised students not to return to school until they had been well for a full day.

St. Francis Prep, a Queens high school, had previously closed in late April because of a flu outbreak. The school later reopened, and the affected students recovered, according to the mayor’s office.

Bloomberg said in a statement that, as city officials had promised when H1N1 first appeared in New York the previous month, they would tell residents what was known while avoiding speculation about unanswered questions.

As of Thursday night, the World Health Organization and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention had confirmed 7,412 H1N1 cases and 63 related deaths worldwide. The CDC reported that the United States accounted for 4,298 confirmed infections and three deaths. Of those cases, 224 were in New York. It remained uncertain whether the five infections announced by Bloomberg and other state and city officials were already reflected in the CDC’s latest figures.

# BREAKING NEWS: New York City closes three Queens schools after new H1N1 cases

**NEW YORK** — New York City officials ordered three public schools in Queens to close after five new cases of the H1N1 influenza virus were confirmed, authorities announced Thursday.

The closures affect Intermediate School 238 in Hollis, Public School 16 in Corona and Intermediate School 5 in Elmhurst. Officials said the campuses had reported unusually high numbers of students with flu-like symptoms, including fever, coughing and sore throat.

The five confirmed cases were connected to I.S. 238, where an assistant principal was hospitalized in critical condition with symptoms consistent with H1N1, then widely known as swine flu.

Mayor Michael Bloomberg said the closures were a precaution intended to limit transmission. Health officials were monitoring students and staff members and urged anyone experiencing symptoms to remain home and contact a medical provider.

The schools were expected to remain closed for several days while buildings were cleaned and health authorities assessed whether the virus had spread further.

H1N1 had already prompted scattered school closures across the United States. Federal and local health officials stressed that most cases had been mild but warned that people with underlying medical conditions could face a greater risk of serious illness.

**New York City — May 14, 2009:** Mayor Michael Bloomberg announced that three Queens public schools would close temporarily after unusually large numbers of students developed flu-like symptoms, as officials tried to slow transmission of the new H1N1 “swine flu” virus.

The schools were:

- **Intermediate School 238 in Hollis:** four students had confirmed H1N1 infections. On Thursday, **241 students were absent**, and the school nurse had seen **23 sick students**. An assistant principal was hospitalized in critical condition with suspected H1N1.
- **Public School 16 in Corona:** the nurse saw **29 students with flu-like symptoms**, far above the usual five to ten daily visits.
- **Intermediate School 5 in Elmhurst:** about **80 students reported to the nurse with flu-like symptoms**, compared with roughly ten on a normal day.

The schools were to close beginning Friday and remain shut for five school days, through the Memorial Day period, with reopening planned for **May 26**.

Bloomberg said the closings were precautionary and based on clusters of illness rather than panic. “We are doing what we said we would do: monitoring the situation and taking action where the facts warrant it,” he said. City Health Commissioner **Dr. Thomas Frieden** said the virus appeared to be spreading more widely, but officials had not detected an increase in its severity. He advised people with fever and respiratory symptoms to remain home and emphasized handwashing and covering coughs.

At the time, the **U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention** reported approximately **4,300 confirmed and probable U.S. cases in 47 states**, with **three deaths**. The **World Health Organization’s May 15 update** listed **7,520 laboratory-confirmed cases in 34 countries and 65 deaths worldwide**.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a detailed news story dated during the 2009 H1N1 outbreak explaining why two intermediate schools and one primary school in Queens are being closed for at least five days.
counterfactuals.output:
**May 14, 2009**

# Three Queens Schools to Close as H1N1 Illness Spreads

**NEW YORK** — City officials announced Thursday that two intermediate schools and one primary school in Queens will close for at least five school days after unusually large numbers of students developed fever and other influenza-like symptoms, raising concern that the new H1N1 virus was spreading rapidly inside the schools.

The affected schools are Intermediate School 238, the Susan B. Anthony School in Hollis; Intermediate School 5, the Walter Crowley School in Elmhurst; and Public School 16 in Corona. Classes are to be suspended beginning Friday, May 15. Officials said the schools would remain closed for a minimum of five school days, with reopening dependent on illness levels and guidance from health authorities.

Mayor Michael R. Bloomberg and city health and education officials said the decision was based not simply on confirmed laboratory tests, but on the size and speed of the outbreaks. Hundreds of children were absent or had visited school nurses with fever, coughing, sore throats and other symptoms associated with influenza.

Concern was especially acute at I.S. 238, where several students had confirmed H1N1 infections and a school employee was reported to be critically ill. The severe adult case, combined with a growing cluster of sick pupils, prompted officials to take the unusual step of shutting the building.

At I.S. 5, officials reported a sharp rise in absenteeism and large numbers of students being sent to the nurse with flu-like symptoms. P.S. 16 was also experiencing an abnormal concentration of respiratory illness. Laboratory confirmation was still pending in some cases, but health officials said they did not need to wait for every child to be tested before acting.

The closures are intended to interrupt close-contact transmission by keeping students and staff apart during the period when infected people are most likely to spread the virus. They also will give school officials time to clean the buildings and allow the Health Department to track new illnesses.

Officials stressed that H1N1 is spread primarily through respiratory droplets and close personal contact, not because a school building remains permanently contaminated. Cleaning alone, they said, would not be enough if sick and exposed students continued to gather in crowded classrooms, cafeterias and hallways.

The decision marked a more targeted approach than the broad closures ordered earlier in the outbreak. In late April, several schools connected to an initial Queens cluster had been closed as authorities tried to determine how widely the new virus was circulating. Since then, federal and local guidance has shifted away from automatically closing a school after a single confirmed case.

Instead, officials are focusing on schools where illness is widespread, absenteeism is unusually high or severe disease has occurred. Most people infected with H1N1 have experienced relatively mild symptoms and recovered without hospitalization, but health authorities warned that influenza can be dangerous, particularly for people with asthma, diabetes, weakened immune systems or other underlying conditions.

Parents were advised to keep children with fever, coughing or sore throats at home and to contact a physician if symptoms became severe. Warning signs include difficulty breathing, chest pain, bluish skin, dehydration, confusion or a fever that improves and then returns.

Children affected by the closures should not simply gather elsewhere, officials said. Families were urged to avoid play groups, parties and other crowded activities that could defeat the purpose of closing the schools.

The city said it would continue monitoring attendance and visits to nurses’ offices throughout the public-school system. The three Queens schools will reopen only after officials determine that the outbreaks have subsided and that students and employees can return safely.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

**NEW YORK (CNN) —** New York City health officials are investigating a suspected flu outbreak at a Queens school, where an assistant principal is critically ill with symptoms consistent with the H1N1 virus.

The administrator, identified by city officials as Mitchell Wiener of Intermediate School 238 in Hollis, was hospitalized after becoming seriously sick. Several students at the school have also reported flu-like symptoms, prompting officials to close the campus as a precaution.

The case has renewed concern in Queens, where St. Francis Preparatory School temporarily closed in April after hundreds of students became ill and dozens were confirmed to have H1N1, commonly called swine flu.

Health authorities are advising students with fever, cough, sore throat or other flu symptoms to remain at home, avoid close contact with others and seek medical care if symptoms become severe. Students should not return to school until they have been fever-free for at least 24 hours without fever-reducing medication, officials said.

As of **May 16, 2009**, the World Health Organization reported **8,451 laboratory-confirmed H1N1 cases in 36 countries, including 72 deaths**. The latest U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention count available at that time listed **4,714 confirmed and probable cases in 47 states and the District of Columbia, with four deaths**.

Officials stressed that most H1N1 infections had been relatively mild but said the administrator’s condition showed that serious complications were possible. Investigators were working to determine how widely the virus had spread within the school community.
